title: Introduction & Licensing
examFocus: Medical requirements, CDL classes, endorsements, restrictions, disqualification rules — tested heavily on GK exam
summary: CDL classes, endorsements, restrictions, medical self-certification, and the disqualification rules examiners love to test.

topics.heading: The three CDL classes
bullets: Class A: any combination with a GCWR of 26,001+ lbs, as long as the towed unit's GVWR is over 10,000 lbs. Think tractor-trailers. Driving a Class A vehicle requires considerably more skill and knowledge than Classes B and C.

Class B: any single vehicle with a GVWR of 26,001+ lbs, or one towing something 10,000 lbs or less. Think straight trucks and large buses. Safely driving these requires more knowledge and skill than Class C vehicles.

Class C: doesn't meet A or B, but is either built for 16+ passengers (including the driver) or carries placarded hazardous materials. Some large Class C vehicles may require more skill than smaller ones, but licensing is based principally on the type of cargo carried.
Licenses stack downward: a Class A license also covers B and C vehicles; a Class B license also covers C.

topics.heading: Endorsements (extra letters on your CDL)
bullets: H – Hazardous materials. Requires a written test plus a TSA fingerprint background check. TSA and DOT require background checks on commercial drivers certified to transport hazardous materials.

N – Tank vehicle. Needed for tanks rated over 119 gallons individually and 1,000+ gallons combined, mounted permanently or temporarily. Liquids in bulk cause driving control problems because cargo is heavy, prone to shifting, and has a high center of gravity.

P – Passenger. Needed to drive any vehicle built to carry 16+ people including the driver. Must pass a special knowledge examination on safety considerations when transporting passengers and must pass skills tests in a passenger vehicle.
S – School bus. Must pass a special knowledge examination on safety considerations when transporting passengers in a school bus and must pass skills tests in a school bus.
T – Doubles/Triples. Considerable additional knowledge and skill is necessary to safely pull double and triple trailers in various traffic conditions.
X – Combination of tank + hazmat (hauling hazardous materials in a tank). Shows you have passed special knowledge examinations for both tank vehicles and hazardous materials.
Only P, S, and N can ever appear on a Commercial Learner's Permit (CLP). A CLP with P or S automatically carries a 'no passengers' restriction; a CLP with N carries a 'no cargo in tank' restriction.

topics.heading: Common restriction codes
bullets: E – no manual transmission (you tested in an automatic). For the skills test and restriction, an automatic transmission includes any transmission not operating fully on the gear shift and clutch principle.
K – intrastate only. If you certify as Non-Excepted Intrastate or Excepted Intrastate, you're restricted from operating a CMV in interstate commerce.

L – no air brakes. If you don't take or fail the air brake component of the knowledge test, or perform the skills test in a vehicle not equipped with air brakes. Air brakes include any braking system operating fully or partially on the air brake principle.
Z – no full air brakes (air-over-hydraulic only).
O – no fifth-wheel tractor-trailer combos (you tested with a pintle hook connection instead).
M – no Class A passenger vehicle (tested in a Class B passenger vehicle).
N – no Class A and B passenger vehicle (tested in a Class C passenger vehicle).
V – a medical variance is on file.

topics.heading: The testing path
bullets: Knowledge tests: general knowledge (everyone), plus air brakes, combination vehicles, passenger, school bus, tank, doubles/triples, or hazmat as needed for your endorsements.
Skills test has three parts, taken in this exact order, and you must pass each before moving on: vehicle inspection, basic vehicle control, then on-road driving.
You must test in the same class and configuration of vehicle you want licensed for.

topics.heading: Medical self-certification
bullets: You must declare interstate vs. intrastate commerce, and excepted vs. non-excepted status, when applying, renewing, upgrading, or transferring a CDL.
Most CDL holders driving in interstate commerce are 'non-excepted interstate' and must submit a current DOT medical examiner's certificate.
Failing to keep a required medical certificate current makes you 'not-certified' and you can lose your CDL.
As of December 11, 2025, medical examiner certificates are submitted electronically by the medical provider to FMCSA — Tax Collector's Offices no longer accept paper certificates.

topics.heading: Drug & Alcohol Clearinghouse (2024 update)
bullets: Beginning November 18, 2024, FLHSMV must obtain your driving record from the Commercial Driver's License Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse when applying, renewing, transferring, or changing a CDL/CLP.
If the Clearinghouse shows you are prohibited from operating a CMV, FLHSMV cannot issue, renew, transfer, or change your CDL/CLP.
FLHSMV must downgrade your CDL/CLP within 60 days of receiving prohibition notification from the Clearinghouse.
You will be notified immediately if prohibited, and you have 20 days to request an informal hearing.

topics.heading: Entry-Level Driver Training (ELDT)
bullets: Since February 7, 2022, entry-level drivers must complete ELDT before taking certain CDL skills or knowledge tests.
ELDT required for: first-time Class A or Class B CDL applicants, upgrading Class B to Class A, and first-time school bus (S), passenger (P), or hazardous materials (H) endorsements.
Training must be from an FMCSA-registered training provider.

topics.heading: Language requirements (2026 update)
bullets: As of February 6, 2026, all driver license knowledge and skills examinations are administered exclusively in English.
This change applies to all driver license classifications, including exams administered orally.
Interpreters may not be used during the administration of any CDL tests.

topics.heading: Residency requirements (2024 update)
bullets: Effective October 7, 2024, all CLP/CDL applicants or those updating an address must provide proof of Florida residency.
You must be a Florida resident to obtain a Florida CDL.

topics.heading: Disqualification numbers worth memorizing
bullets: BAC of 0.04% or higher, refusing an alcohol test, or driving a CMV under the influence of alcohol/drugs: lose your CDL for at least 1 year on a first offense (3 years if hauling placarded hazmat).
A second major offense (DUI, felony with a CMV, leaving the scene, causing a fatality through negligent operation) = disqualified for life.
Out-of-service order violation: 90 days minimum for a first offense, 1 year for a second within 10 years, 3 years for a third+.
Railroad-crossing violation: 60 days for a first offense, 120 days for a second within 3 years, 1 year for a third within 3 years.
Two serious traffic violations in a CMV within 3 years: at least 60 days disqualified. Three or more: at least 120 days.
Serious violations include going 15+ mph over the limit, reckless driving, improper lane changes, following too closely, and driving without the right class/endorsement.

Two or more convictions for using a hand-held phone or texting while driving a CMV: 60 days disqualified for the second offense, 120 for a third+, with fines up to $2,750 for the driver and $11,000 for the carrier.
Using a false name, making a false statement, or concealing a material fact in a CDL application: up to 5 years in prison, $5,000 fine, and suspension of driving privilege for at least 1 year.

topics.heading: Other rules that show up on the test
bullets: You may hold only one driver's license, period.
Notify your employer within 30 days of any traffic conviction (except parking), no matter what vehicle you were driving.
Notify your employer within 2 business days if your license is suspended, revoked, canceled, or you're disqualified.
Give a new employer your driving-job history for the past 10 years.
In Florida: minimum age is 18 for intrastate driving, 21 for interstate or hazmat; you must already hold a Florida Class E license.
It is illegal to permit or authorize an unlicensed person to drive a motor vehicle — can result in 60-day jail sentence and $500 fine for the person who authorizes it.

quiz.q: Total stopping distance is a combination of:
options: Perception distance + reaction distance + braking distance
Reaction distance + viewing distance + braking distance
quiz.explain: Total stopping distance = perception distance (seeing the hazard) + reaction distance (deciding and moving your foot) + braking distance (actual stopping once brakes apply).

quiz.q: What factors determine your selection of a starting gear?
options: Flatness or grade of the road, load, and valve
Flatness or grade of the road, load, and engine
Weight of the vehicle, tire type, and speed
Weather, cargo, and gear ratio only
quiz.explain: Choose a starting gear based on the flatness or grade of the road, your load, and whether the road is slippery. Lower gears are needed on hills, with heavy loads, or on slippery surfaces.

quiz.q: Why should you be in the proper gear before starting down a hill?
options: You will not be able to shift into a lower gear once you are going down the hill
Because the clutch is designed for level ground
There is no need to do this
To prevent the engine from overheating
quiz.explain: You must downshift before starting down a hill. Once speed builds up you will not be able to shift into a lower gear, and you may lose all engine braking effect.

quiz.q: What type of vehicles can get stuck on a railroad crossing?
options: Low-slung units such as lowboys, car carriers, moving vans, and possum-belly livestock trailers
Only long tractor-trailers with tandem axles
Only double and triple trailer combinations
quiz.explain: Low-slung units (lowboy, car carrier, moving van, possum-belly livestock trailer) and single-axle tractors with long trailers can hang up on raised railroad crossings.

quiz.q: Describe the proper braking technique when stopping with air brakes.
options: Use the same braking technique you always have; only fully apply the brakes in an emergency stop if you have working ABS on all axles
Always push the brake pedal all the way to the floor on every stop
Pump the brake pedal rapidly on every stop
Never use the service brakes, only engine braking
quiz.explain: With air brakes, control the pressure so the vehicle stops smoothly. In an emergency with working ABS on all axles, you can fully apply the brakes.

quiz.q: How long does it take for a typical tractor-trailer to clear a double track?
quiz.explain: It takes a typical tractor-trailer at least 14 seconds to clear a single track and more than 15 seconds to clear a double track.Railroad crossings should be approached with the expectation that a train is coming.

quiz.q: What are some advantages of going right off the road rather than trying to stop in a hurry?
options: You avoid a head-on collision, gain an escape route, and no one is likely to be driving on the shoulder
You can stop faster on the shoulder
It lets other drivers pass you more easily
quiz.explain: Going right avoids forcing anyone into oncoming traffic and a possible head-on collision. Most shoulders are strong enough to support a large vehicle and offer an escape route.

quiz.q: What are the slack adjusters?
options: Part of your air brake system used to adjust the brakes to ensure they are safe
Devices that hold the trailer to the tractor
Springs that release the parking brake
Valves that control the air supply
quiz.explain: Slack adjusters are an important part of the air brake system that allow you to adjust the brakes. On drum brakes they sit between the push rod and S-cam; on disc brakes between the power screw and push rod.

quiz.q: How can you check slack adjusters?
options: Pull hard on each slack adjuster you can reach while wearing gloves; they should not have more than about one inch of 'give'
Press the brake pedal and listen for noises
quiz.explain: Use gloves and pull hard on each reachable slack adjuster. If there is an inch or more of 'give', the brakes should be adjusted.

quiz.q: How can you test the low pressure warning signal?
options: Shut the engine off, turn the key back on, and step on and off the brake pedal to reduce air pressure; the warning signal must come on before pressure drops below 55 psi
Drain all the air from the tanks
Listen for air leaking around the wheels
quiz.explain: With the engine off and key on, pump the brake pedal to lower air pressure. The low air pressure warning light/buzzer must activate before the pressure drops below 55 psi in either system.

quiz.q: How can you check that the spring brakes come on automatically?
options: Keep stepping on and off the brake pedal to lower air pressure until the parking brake valve pops out on both tractor-trailer and single vehicles
Only check them at the shop
Push the brake pedal all the way to the floor
quiz.explain: Continue the same method used to test the low air pressure warning, stepping on and off the brake pedal, until pressure drops low enough that the spring brakes automatically deploy and the parking brake valve pops out.

quiz.q: What are the maximum leakage rates?
options: Single vehicle: 3 psi in 1 minute; combination vehicle: 4 psi in 1 minute; air-over-hydraulic and any trailer: 2 psi in 1 minute
No more than 1 psi in 5 minutes
quiz.explain: Maximum air leakage rates: 3 psi in one minute for single vehicles, 4 psi in one minute for combination vehicles, and 2 psi in one minute for air-over-hydraulic brakes and trailers.

quiz.q: Define the danger zone. How far does the
options: The danger zone is the area around the bus where students are in the most danger; it extends 10 feet from the front, sides, and rear of the bus
The danger zone is 5 feet from the bus
The danger zone is 100 feet from the bus
The danger zone only covers the driver's side
quiz.explain: The danger zone is the area around the bus where students are most at risk, extending about 10 feet from the front, sides, and rear of the bus. Students should stay well away from these areas.

quiz.q: Having two axles and a gross vehicle weight
options: What qualifies a vehicle for the International Registration Plan? A Qualified Vehicle has two axles and a gross vehicle weight over 26,000 pounds, or three or more axles regardless of weight
What qualifies a vehicle for a Class B CDL
What qualifies a vehicle for an endorsement
What qualifies a vehicle as a recreational vehicle
quiz.explain: For IRP purposes, a Qualified Vehicle is any power unit used in two or more member jurisdictions with two axles and a gross weight over 26,000 pounds, or three or more axles regardless of weight, or a combination over 26,000 pounds.

quiz.q: What factors determine your selection of a
options: Total weight of the vehicle and cargo, length and steepness of the grade, road conditions, and weather
quiz.explain: When going down a long, steep downgrade, your safe speed depends on the total weight of the vehicle and cargo, the length and steepness of the grade, road conditions, and weather.

quiz.q: Which shut-off valves should be open and
options: All shut-off valves should be open except those at the rear of the last trailer, which should be closed
All shut-off valves should be closed
Only the valves at the rear of the first trailer
The valves at the front should be closed
quiz.explain: All shut-off valves should be in the open position except the ones at the back of the last trailer, which should be closed.

quiz.q: Is used in combination, when the weight of
options: What qualifies a vehicle for IFTA registration? A Qualified Motor Vehicle is used in combination when the weight of such combination exceeds 26,000 pounds
What qualifies a vehicle for Class C
What qualifies a vehicle for an exemption
What qualifies a vehicle for the P endorsement
quiz.explain: For IFTA, a Qualified Motor Vehicle has two axles and a gross weight exceeding 26,000 pounds, or is used in combination when the weight of the combination exceeds 26,000 pounds. Recreational vehicles are excluded.

quiz.q: Should a tank vehicle take curves, on
options: No, tank vehicles should slow down before curves, on ramps, and off ramps to keep from rolling over
Yes, at the posted speed limit
quiz.explain: Tank vehicles should slow down before curves, on ramps, and off ramps. A safe speed for other vehicles may be too fast for a tanker because the liquid moves and raises the center of gravity.

quiz.q: What are some advantages of going right
options: You avoid oncoming traffic and a possible head-on collision, and people are less likely to be driving on the shoulder
quiz.explain: Moving right avoids forcing anyone into opposing traffic lanes and a possible head-on collision. No one is likely to be driving on the shoulder, making it a safer escape route.

quiz.q: What should you be able to see if the
options: With flat mirrors you should see the side of the bus and the rear tires; convex mirrors give a wider view and show the danger zone; crossover mirrors show the front bumper area and the ground directly in front of the bus
quiz.explain: Flat mirrors should show the side of the bus and rear tires. Convex mirrors show a wider area including the danger zone. Crossover mirrors show the front bumper area and the ground in front of the bus.

quiz.q: What is an "escape ramp?"
options: A ramp leading to a long bed of loose, soft material to slow a runaway vehicle, sometimes in combination with an upgrade
Another term for an off ramp
A ramp used to pass another vehicle
quiz.explain: An escape ramp is a long bed of loose, soft material (like gravel) used to slow and stop a runaway vehicle, sometimes combined with an upgrade. Know their locations on your route.

quiz.q: How can you test the low pressure warning
options: Shut the engine off, turn the key back on, and step on and off the brake pedal; the warning must come on before the pressure drops below 55 psi
Pump the pedal while racing the engine
There is no way to test it
quiz.explain: With the engine off and key on, pump the brake pedal to reduce air pressure. The low air pressure warning must activate before pressure drops below 55 psi.

quiz.q: How do you check to make sure trailer height
options: Make sure the trailer is low enough that the fifth wheel will engage the kingpin but high enough to clear the front of the trailer nose during coupling
There is no need to check it
Raise the trailer as high as it will go
Lower it until it touches the ground
quiz.explain: The trailer height must be set so the kingpin will engage the fifth wheel correctly: not so high it won't latch, and not so low the tractor strikes the trailer nose.

quiz.q: If a tire blows out, you should put the brakes
options: Hold the steering wheel firmly and stay off the brake until the vehicle slows, then brake gently and pull off the road
Put the brakes on hard to stop quickly
Let go of the steering wheel
quiz.explain: On a tire blowout, hold the steering wheel firmly and stay off the brake until the vehicle slows down, then brake very gently and pull off the road.

quiz.q: If you are away from your vehicle only a short
options: You must still apply the parking brake and, if needed, chock the wheels even for a short time
You do not need to use the parking brake
Only use the parking brake on hills
Leave it in gear and walk away
quiz.explain: Any time you leave your vehicle even briefly, apply the parking brake and chock the wheels if necessary. Never leave a vehicle unattended without the parking brakes set.

quiz.q: What three things determine how much
options: The weight of the liquid, the amount of liquid you can load based on weight and expansion room, and the legal weight limits for the vehicle
quiz.explain: How much liquid you can load depends on the weight of the liquid, the amount you can legally carry based on the vehicle's weight limits, and the space needed for expansion (outage).

quiz.q: What type of vehicles can get stuck on a
options: Low-slung units such as lowboys, car carriers, moving vans, and possum-belly livestock trailers
quiz.explain: Low-slung units (lowboy, car carrier, moving van, possum-belly livestock trailer) and single-axle tractors with long trailers can hang up on raised railroad crossings.

quiz.q: You are unloading students along your
options: Students should walk at least 10 feet (about 5 giant steps) in front of the bus, cross to the left, and wait for the driver's signal before crossing
Students should cross immediately behind the bus
Students should stay on the bus
Students should run across the road
quiz.explain: After exiting, students should go to a point at least 10 feet in front of the bus (out of the danger zone), cross to the left side, and wait for the driver's signal before crossing.

quiz.q: Front wheel brakes are good under all
quiz.explain: Front wheel brakes are not good under all conditions. On slippery surfaces locking the front wheels causes loss of steering control. This is why some vehicles route more braking to the rear.

quiz.q: How can you check that the spring brakes come
options: Keep stepping on and off the brake pedal until the spring brakes deploy and the parking brake valve pops out
Check them visually at the shop
quiz.explain: Continue the method used for the low air pressure warning: step on and off the brake pedal until pressure drops enough that the spring brakes automatically come on and the valve pops out.

quiz.q: How long does it take for a typical tractor-trailer
options: More than 15 seconds to clear a double track and 14 seconds for a single track
quiz.explain: It takes a typical tractor-trailer at least 14 seconds to clear a single track and more than 15 seconds to clear a double track.

quiz.q: What do you check when making a visual
options: Check that the fifth wheel is fully engaged on the kingpin by looking into the back of the fifth wheel, and that the locking jaws are closed
quiz.explain: When checking coupling visually, look into the back of the fifth wheel to confirm it is locked onto the kingpin and the locking jaws are closed.

quiz.q: How do you know if your vehicle is
options: Vehicles have a yellow ABS malfunction lamp on the instrument panel; trailers have one on the left side near the front or rear corner
quiz.explain: ABS-equipped trucks/buses have a yellow ABS malfunction lamp on the instrument panel. Trailers have a yellow lamp on the left side, on the front or rear corner. Dollies built after March 1, 1998 must have one on the left side.

quiz.q: How should you brake when you drive a
options: Brake the same way you always have, using only the braking force necessary to stop safely and stay in control
Push the brake pedal hard on every stop
quiz.explain: With ABS, brake the same way you always have. Use only the braking force necessary, and in an emergency with working ABS on all axles you can fully apply the brakes.

quiz.q: What position should students be in front of
options: At least 10 feet directly in front of the bus, out of the danger zone, so the driver can see them
quiz.explain: Students should be at least 10 feet directly in front of the bus, out of the danger zone and in plain view of the driver, before they cross.

quiz.q: Why should you pull a dolly out from under a
options: So you can reach the shut-off valves and avoid damaging the dolly or the trailer when you disconnect them
quiz.explain: You should pull the dolly out from under the trailer before disconnecting it from the trailer in front so you can reach and operate the shut-off valves and prevent damage during uncoupling.

quiz.q: How do antilock brakes help you?
options: They keep your wheels from locking up and help you maintain control during hard braking so you can steer around obstacles
quiz.explain: ABS prevents wheel lockup, helping you keep control and steer around obstacles during hard braking. ABS does not necessarily shorten stopping distance or increase stopping power.

quiz.q: What should you check for when inspecting
options: Check the converter dolly for secure coupling, spring brakes, air lines, glad hands, safety chains, and the pintle hook for wear or damage
quiz.explain: When inspecting a converter dolly, check the frame, drawbar, pintle hook, glad hands and air lines, safety chains, couplers, and tires for wear, damage, and secure mounting.

quiz.q: What two reasons make special care
options: The high center of gravity of the liquid cargo and the surge/free surface effect that makes handling difficult
The vehicle is harder to steer at low speed
quiz.explain: Special care is needed with tank vehicles because the liquid cargo has a high center of gravity and because surge (liquid sloshing) makes the vehicle harder to control.

quiz.q: You still have normal brake functions if your
options: ABS is not working; you still have normal brake functions and should drive normally but get the ABS serviced soon
ABS fails so you have no brakes
quiz.explain: If ABS malfunctions, you still have your regular brakes. Drive and brake normally but have the ABS system serviced soon.

quiz.q: Should the shut-off valves on the rear of the
options: The shut-off valves on the rear of the last trailer should be closed; all others should be open
All shut-off valves should be closed
All shut-off valves should be open
Only the front should be closed
quiz.explain: All shut-off valves should be open except those on the rear of the last trailer, which should be closed.

quiz.q: What is a passive highway-rail crossing?
options: A crossing with no gates, flashing lights, or bells; it only has a passive warning sign, so you must be extra cautious and look for trains yourself
quiz.explain: A passive highway-rail crossing has no active warning devices (no gates, flashing lights, or bells) - only signs. Because there is no signal, you must slow down and look for trains yourself.

quiz.q: How do you know if your converter dolly is
options: Dollies manufactured on or after March 1, 1998 are required to have an ABS lamp on the left side; check for the yellow malfunction lamp and look for the ECU and wheel speed sensor wires under the unit
quiz.explain: Converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998 must have an ABS lamp on the left side. For older units, look under the vehicle for the ECU and wheel speed sensor wires.

quiz.q: Do not apply the brake while you are turning. It's
options: very easy to lock your wheels while turning, which could cause a skid out of control
quiz.explain: Do not apply the brake while turning because it is very easy to lock the wheels and skid out of control. Slow down before the turn instead.

quiz.q: Do not brake harshly. Brake smoothly using steady
options: pressure so students and passengers are not thrown forward
quiz.explain: When carrying passengers or students, brake smoothly with steady pressure so you don't throw people forward or cause injury.

quiz.q: Do not change lanes while proceeding through the
quiz.explain: Do not change lanes while proceeding through an intersection or railroad crossing. Keep your path steady so other drivers can anticipate your movements.

quiz.q: Do not grind or clash gears.
options: Double-clutch or use the correct technique to shift smoothly and prevent transmission damage
quiz.explain: Grinding or clashing gears damages the transmission and can cause you to lose control. Shift using proper double-clutch or smooth shifting technique.

quiz.q: Do not let your vehicle roll.
options: Use the brakes and parking brake so the vehicle does not roll backward or forward, especially when starting on a hill or when stopped
quiz.explain: Never let your vehicle roll. Hold it with the brakes and parking brake until you are ready to move, especially on grades where rollback can cause a crash.

quiz.q: Do not move a student you believe may have
options: been seriously injured; wait for qualified medical help unless there is danger of fire or passing traffic
quiz.explain: Do not move a seriously injured student unless there is a danger of fire or passing traffic. Moving them could make injuries worse; wait for qualified help.

quiz.q: Do not over or under steer the vehicle.
options: Steer smoothly and correctly so you keep the bus in the proper lane and avoid skids or rollovers
quiz.explain: Over or under steering can cause loss of control. Steer smoothly and precisely to keep the vehicle in the correct path, especially when carrying passengers.

quiz.q: Do not put vehicle over curbs, sidewalks, or lane
options: markings when turning or parking, as it can damage the vehicle and endanger pedestrians
quiz.explain: Do not drive over curbs, sidewalks, or lane markings. Doing so can damage the vehicle, violate the law, and endanger pedestrians.

title: Driving Safely
examFocus: The bulk of the General Knowledge test — inspection, control, space management, speed, hazards, night/weather, emergencies, ABS, skids, fires, alcohol
summary: The biggest section on the general knowledge test: inspection, control, space, speed, hazards, night/weather driving, emergencies, ABS, skids, fires, and alcohol.

topics.heading: Vehicle inspection basics
bullets: The seven-step method: approach & look underneath, check the engine compartment, start the engine & check the cab, kill the engine & check lights, walk around the vehicle, check signal lights, do the final brake checks.
Air pressure should build from 50 to 90 psi within 3 minutes on older single systems; the governor cuts out around 120-140 psi.
Minimum tread depth: 4/32 inch on steering (front) tires, 2/32 inch on all other tires.
More than 10 degrees of steering wheel play (about 2 inches of movement at the rim) is a problem.
Required emergency gear: fire extinguisher, spare electrical fuses (unless you have circuit breakers), and 3 reflective triangles (or 6 fusees or 3 liquid-burning flares).
Hydraulic brake check: pump the pedal 3 times, then hold firm pressure for 5 seconds — the pedal should not move.
Cargo securement must be re-checked within the first 50 miles, then every 150 miles or 3 hours, whichever comes first.

topics.heading: Basic control & shifting
bullets: When backing, always try to back toward the driver's side so you can see; use a helper and agree on a stop signal beforehand.
Downshift before you start down a hill or enter a curve — never after your speed has already built up.
Most heavy vehicles with unsynchronized manual transmissions require double-clutching; synchronized transmissions don't.
Turn retarders OFF whenever the road is wet, icy, or snow-covered — they can make the drive wheels skid.

topics.heading: Seeing & communicating
bullets: Look 12-15 seconds ahead — about one block in the city, a quarter mile on the highway.
Check mirrors regularly, and always before, during, and after a lane change, turn, or merge.
Signal early, hold the signal through the maneuver, and cancel it right after.

If you must stop on the road, place warning triangles within 10 minutes: on a two-lane road, one within 10 feet of the vehicle and one each 100 feet ahead and behind; on a divided or one-way road, at 10, 100, and 200 feet toward oncoming traffic. If a hill or curve blocks your visibility, move the back triangle to keep at least 500 feet of advance warning.

topics.heading: Speed & stopping distance
bullets: Total stopping distance = perception distance + reaction distance + braking distance.
At 55 mph in ideal conditions, total stopping distance is roughly 419 feet — nearly a football field and a half.
Doubling your speed roughly quadruples your stopping distance and impact force; tripling your speed multiplies both by about 9.
Cut speed by about a third on a wet road, by half or more on packed snow, and down to a crawl on ice.
Hydroplaning can happen at speeds as low as 30 mph if there's enough standing water.

topics.heading: Managing space
bullets: Following distance rule: 1 second for every 10 feet of your vehicle's length at speeds under 40 mph, plus 1 extra second if you're over 40 mph.
A loaded vehicle sits lower than an empty one of the same type — clearing a bridge loaded doesn't guarantee you'll clear it empty.
On right turns, keep the rear of your vehicle close to the curb rather than swinging wide left first — swinging left invites someone to pass you on the right.

topics.heading: Distracted, drowsy & impaired driving
bullets: Hand-held phone use and texting are both banned while driving a CMV. A second conviction means 60 days disqualified; a third means 120 days, plus fines up to $2,750 for the driver and $11,000 for the carrier.
Getting 6 hours of sleep or less roughly triples your crash risk.
Plan breaks about every 100 miles or 2 hours on long trips — the only real cure for drowsiness is sleep, not caffeine or fresh air.

topics.heading: Night, fog & winter driving
bullets: Low beams show the road about 250 feet ahead; high beams about 350-500 feet. Never outdrive your headlights.
Dim your high beams within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle or one you're following.
The best advice for fog is simply: don't drive in it. If you must, use low beams and fog lights, not high beams.
Winter tread minimums are the same as always — 4/32 inch front, 2/32 inch other — but more is safer.

topics.heading: Railroad crossings
bullets: The round, black-on-yellow sign is the advance warning sign — it means slow down and be ready to stop.
If there's no stop line, stop between 15 and 50 feet from the nearest rail at a cross-buck sign.
A typical tractor-trailer needs about 14 seconds to clear a single track, and 15+ seconds to clear a double track — never get trapped stopping on the tracks.
Never shift gears while crossing the tracks.

topics.heading: Mountain driving & brake fade
bullets: Select your safe speed and downshift to the right gear BEFORE starting down a grade, not after you're already rolling.
Use engine braking as your main speed control; apply the brakes firmly enough for a real slowdown, then release — repeated hard, continuous braking causes brake fade.
Escape ramps use soft material (and often an upgrade) to safely stop a runaway vehicle — use one if your brakes fail.

topics.heading: Emergency maneuvers, ABS & skids
bullets: Steering around an obstacle is often faster and safer than trying to stop in time.
Controlled braking: brake as hard as possible without locking the wheels. Stab braking: brake fully, release the instant wheels lock, then reapply.
If a tire blows out, hold the wheel firmly and stay off the brake until you've slowed down — braking hard can cause loss of control.
ABS does not necessarily shorten stopping distance — it helps you keep steering control. Brake the same way you always would; don't pump the brakes.
To recover from a drive-wheel skid: stop braking to let the wheels roll again, and counter-steer. Never use the trailer hand valve to try to straighten a skidding trailer.

topics.heading: Accidents, fires & alcohol
bullets: Three steps at any accident: protect the area, notify authorities, care for the injured.
Fire extinguisher classes: A = wood/paper/ordinary combustibles, B = flammable liquids, C = electrical, D = combustible metals. Never use water on an electrical or gasoline fire.
A standard drink is about 12 oz of beer, 5 oz of wine, or 1.5 oz of 80-proof liquor — they all contain roughly the same amount of alcohol.
The liver only processes about one drink per hour; only time sobers you up, not coffee or a cold shower.

bullets: There are 9 hazard classes. A placarded vehicle needs 4 identical placards: front, rear, and both sides.
You need a hazmat endorsement to legally drive a vehicle that requires placards.

title: Transporting Cargo Safely
examFocus: Cargo securement, weight distribution, and inspection — covered on General Knowledge exam
summary: Weight limits, balance, tie-downs, and special cargo that needs extra care.

topics.heading: Your responsibilities as the driver
bullets: Inspect your cargo, recognize overloads or poor weight balance, confirm it's properly secured, and make sure it doesn't block your view or your access to emergency equipment.
Re-inspect cargo and tie-downs within the first 50 miles of a trip, and then every 150 miles or 3 hours after that, whichever comes first.

topics.heading: Weight definitions
bullets: GVWR (Gross Vehicle Weight Rating): manufacturer's max loaded weight for one vehicle.
GCWR (Gross Combination Weight Rating): manufacturer's max loaded weight for a power unit plus everything it's towing.
Axle weight: weight transmitted to the ground by one axle or set of axles.
A bridge formula sets lower maximum axle weights for axles that sit closer together, to protect bridges and roads.

topics.heading: Keep it low and balanced
bullets: A high center of gravity (cargo piled high, or heavy cargo on top) makes rollover far more likely, especially in curves.
Too much weight on the steering axle makes steering hard; too little makes it dangerously light and hard to control.
Too little weight on the drive axles causes poor traction and wheel spin, especially in bad weather.

topics.heading: Securing cargo
bullets: Blocking and bracing keep cargo from sliding forward, back, or side to side.
Rule of thumb: at least one tie-down for every 10 feet of cargo, with a minimum of two tie-downs no matter how small the load.
Header boards ('headache racks') protect the cab from cargo sliding forward in a crash or hard stop.
Cover cargo both to protect people from spills and to protect the cargo from weather.

topics.heading: Cargo that needs extra caution
bullets: Dry bulk tanks: high center of gravity — go slow and easy through curves and turns.
Hanging meat: very unstable with a high center of gravity — slow way down on ramps and curves.
Livestock: can shift their weight, especially leaning into curves — use false bulkheads with a partial load.
Oversized loads: require special permits, signage, and sometimes escorts.

title: Transporting Passengers Safely
summary: Bus-specific inspection points, loading rules, hazmat limits on a bus, and the prohibited practices list.

topics.heading: Getting the P endorsement
bullets: Requires a knowledge test covering Sections 2 and 4 of the manual, plus Section 5 (air brakes) if your bus has them, and the passenger skills tests.

topics.heading: Extra inspection points for buses
bullets: Check handholds, railings, floor covering, emergency exit handles, and any restroom emergency buzzer.
Never drive with an open emergency exit door or window, and the 'Emergency Exit' sign must be clearly visible.

topics.heading: Hazardous materials on a bus
bullets: Buses may carry small-arms ammunition (ORM-D labeled), emergency hospital supplies, and drugs.

Buses can never carry: poison gas, more than 100 lbs of solid Class 6 poisons, explosives in a space occupied by people (except small-arms ammo), or labeled radioactive materials in a space occupied by people.
The overall limit for permitted hazardous materials on a bus is 500 lbs total, no more than 100 lbs of any single class.

topics.heading: The standee line
bullets: On buses designed to allow standing, a 2-inch line marks how far forward riders may stand. No one may stand ahead of the rear of the driver's seat.

topics.heading: Railroad crossings & drawbridges
bullets: Stop your bus between 15 and 50 feet before a railroad crossing, listen and look both ways, and open the forward door if it helps you see or hear.
Stop at least 50 feet before an unguarded drawbridge and make sure the draw is fully closed before crossing.

title: Air Brakes
examFocus: CRITICAL for bucket trucks and dump trucks — entire Air Brakes test (25 questions) is based on this section
summary: Every pressure number, timing, and warning threshold the air brake test is built around.

topics.heading: Three systems in one
bullets: Service brakes: the normal brakes you use with the pedal during driving.
Parking brakes: hold the vehicle when parked, using spring pressure held back by air pressure.
Emergency brakes: use parts of the service and parking brake systems to stop the vehicle if the air brake system fails.

topics.heading: The pressure numbers to memorize
bullets: Governor cuts out (stops the compressor) around 125 psi and cuts back in around 100 psi.
The safety relief valve is usually set to open at 150 psi — if it ever releases air, something's wrong.
Low air pressure warning must activate before air pressure drops below 55 psi (or one-half the governor cut-out pressure on older vehicles).
Spring brakes activate fully somewhere in the 20-45 psi range (typically 20-30 psi) — don't wait for them; stop safely the moment the low air warning comes on.
On large buses, low pressure warning devices often signal at 80-85 psi.
Dual air systems should build from 85 to 100 psi within 45 seconds with the engine running; older single air systems build 50 to 90 psi within 3 minutes at idle.

topics.heading: Leak-rate limits (the exact numbers examiners ask about)
bullets: With the engine off and brakes released, air loss should be less than 2 psi/minute for a single vehicle, less than 3 psi/minute for a combination vehicle.
With the foot brake held down for 1 minute, loss should be no more than 3 psi/minute (single vehicle) or 4 psi/minute (combination vehicle).

topics.heading: Slack adjusters & brake types
bullets: If a slack adjuster moves more than about 1 inch when pulled by hand, it likely needs adjustment.
Vehicles built since 1994 have automatic slack adjusters, but you should still check them — don't rely on manual adjustment as a real fix.
S-cam drum brakes are the most common type — air pressure pushes the rod out, moving the slack adjuster and twisting the brake camshaft.
Wedge brakes: the brake chamber push rod pushes a wedge directly between the ends of two brake shoes.
Disc brakes: air pressure acts on a brake chamber and slack adjuster, but a 'power screw' clamps the disc between brake lining pads like a large c-clamp.
Wedge brakes and disc brakes are less common than s-cam brakes.

topics.heading: Brake fade & overheating
bullets: Brake fade happens from overheating; brakes out of adjustment fail first, overloading the rest and accelerating fade.
If the application pressure gauge shows you need to increase pressure to hold the same speed, your brakes are fading — slow down and use a lower gear.
Increased application pressure can also be caused by brakes out of adjustment, air leaks, or mechanical problems.

topics.heading: Stopping distance with air brakes
bullets: Air brakes add 'brake lag' — about half a second, or roughly 32 feet at 55 mph — on top of the usual perception + reaction + braking distance.

topics.heading: Using air brakes correctly
bullets: Never push the brake pedal down while the spring (parking) brakes are set — it can damage them from combined spring and air pressure forces.
Never use the parking brake if the brakes are extremely hot or extremely wet in freezing weather.
Drain air tanks daily unless you have automatic drains — water can freeze in cold weather and cause brake failure.
Compressed air contains water and compressor oil which collect at the bottom of tanks and must be drained.
Some systems have an alcohol evaporator to reduce ice risk in cold weather — check the alcohol container daily during cold weather.
Pressing and releasing the pedal unnecessarily lets air out faster than the compressor can replace it — if pressure gets too low, brakes won't work.

topics.heading: Front brake limiting valves (older vehicles)
bullets: Some vehicles built before 1975 have a front brake limiting valve with 'normal' and 'slippery' positions.
The 'slippery' position cuts normal air pressure to front brakes by half to reduce skid risk.
However, limiting valves actually reduce stopping power — front wheel braking is good under all conditions.
Tests show front wheel skids from braking are not likely even on ice — keep the control in 'normal' position.
Many newer vehicles have automatic front wheel limiting valves that reduce air to front brakes except during hard braking (55+ psi application).

topics.heading: ABS requirements
bullets: Truck tractors with air brakes built on or after March 1, 1997 must have ABS.
Other air brake vehicles (trucks, buses, trailers, converter dollies) built on or after March 1, 1998 must have ABS.
Vehicles with ABS have yellow malfunction lamps — tractors/trucks/buses on the instrument panel, trailers on the left side front or rear corner.
On newer vehicles, the ABS lamp comes on at start-up for bulb check then goes out quickly; on older systems it may stay on until driving over 5 mph.
If the ABS lamp stays on after bulb check or comes on while driving, you may have lost ABS control at one or more wheels.
ABS is an addition to normal brakes — it doesn't decrease or increase normal braking capability and only activates when wheels are about to lock up.

title: Combination Vehicles
examFocus: CRITICAL for pulling trailers — entire Combination Vehicles test (20 questions) is based on this section
summary: Rollover and crack-the-whip risk, trailer air brake parts, and the coupling/uncoupling sequence.

topics.heading: Rollover risk
bullets: More than half of truck driver deaths in crashes are the result of truck rollovers.
Fully loaded rigs are about 10 times more likely to roll over in a crash than empty ones.
Keep cargo low and centered, and slow way down before curves, ramps, and turns — most rollovers happen because of too much speed in a turn, not bad luck.
Keeping cargo low is even more important in combination vehicles than in straight trucks.
If the load is to one side so it makes a trailer lean, a rollover is more likely — make sure cargo is centered and spread out as much as possible.

topics.heading: Crack-the-whip (rearward amplification)
bullets: A quick lane change can whip the rear trailer sideways hard enough to roll it over — many accidents involve only the trailer overturning.
Rearward amplification of 2.0 means the rear trailer is twice as likely to turn over as the tractor.
Triples have a rearward amplification of 3.5 — the last trailer is about 3.5 times as likely to roll as a five-axle tractor.
Steer gently and smoothly when pulling trailers — sudden steering movements can tip the trailer over.
Follow far enough behind other vehicles: at least 1 second for each 10 feet of vehicle length, plus another second if going over 40 mph.

topics.heading: Empty vs. loaded braking
bullets: Large combination vehicles take longer to stop when they are empty than when they are fully loaded.
When lightly loaded, very stiff suspension springs and strong brakes give poor traction and make it very easy to lock up the wheels.
Your trailer can swing out and strike other vehicles when lightly loaded.
Your tractor can jackknife very quickly when lightly loaded.
Bobtail tractors (tractors without semitrailers) are very hard to stop smoothly — tests show they take longer to stop than a tractor-semitrailer loaded to maximum gross weight.

topics.heading: Off-tracking & backing
bullets: The rear wheels follow a tighter path than the front wheels in a turn (off-tracking) — steer wide enough that the rear doesn't run over curbs or pedestrians, but keep the rear close to the curb to block others from passing on the right.
When backing a trailer, turn the steering wheel the OPPOSITE direction from a normal vehicle — and once the trailer starts turning, reverse your input to follow it.

topics.heading: Trailer air brake components
bullets: Trailer hand valve (trolley valve / Johnson bar): use ONLY to test trailer brakes, never while actually driving or for parking.
Tractor protection valve: closes automatically if air pressure drops into the 20-45 psi range, protecting the tractor's own air supply.
Trailer air supply control: a red, 8-sided knob — push in to supply air, pull out to shut off air and apply the trailer's emergency brakes.

Two air lines run to the trailer: the service line (also called the control/signal line) and the emergency line (also called the supply line). Losing pressure in the emergency line sets the trailer's emergency brakes.
Glad hand colors: blue = service line, red = emergency (supply) line.

topics.heading: Railroad-highway crossings with trailers
bullets: Trailers with low underneath clearance can get stuck on raised railroad crossings.
Low slung units at risk: lowboy, car carrier, moving van, possum-belly livestock trailer.
Single-axle tractor pulling a long trailer with landing gear set for a tandem-axle tractor can also get stuck.
If you get stuck, you may not have enough clearance to cross — check crossing height before attempting.

topics.heading: Shut-off valves
bullets: Shut-off valves (cut-out cocks) at the back of trailers must be OPEN — except at the very back of the last trailer in a combination, which must be CLOSED.

topics.heading: Coupling checks that matter
bullets: After coupling, there should be NO visible gap between the upper and lower fifth wheel — a gap means something is wrong.
Pull gently forward with the trailer brakes locked to confirm the kingpin is actually locked in.
Raise the landing gear fully before driving — never drive with it only partway up.

topics.heading: ABS on trailers
bullets: Trailers and converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998 are required to have ABS, shown by a yellow malfunction lamp on the left side of the trailer.

title: Doubles and Triples
summary: Trailer order, converter dolly basics, and the shut-off valve pattern for multiple trailers.

topics.heading: Loading order
bullets: For the safest handling, put the heavier semitrailer in the FIRST position (right behind the tractor) and the lighter trailer in the rear.
Doubles and triples need more following distance and bigger gaps to enter or cross traffic — they're longer and cannot stop or turn as quickly.

topics.heading: Converter dollies
bullets: A converter dolly is one or two axles with a fifth wheel, used to couple an additional semitrailer behind the first one.
Converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998 must have ABS, shown by a yellow lamp on the left side of the dolly.

topics.heading: Shut-off valve pattern (multiple trailers)
bullets: Open at the rear of every trailer EXCEPT the very last one in the combination, which must be closed.
When checking, you should hear air escaping at each open point when the system is charged — confirming air reaches every trailer.

topics.heading: Coupling/uncoupling extra care
bullets: Never unlock the pintle hook while the converter dolly is still positioned under the rear trailer — the tow bar can fly up and cause injury.
Check trailer height carefully before backing a dolly under a trailer; it should sit slightly below the trailer's fifth wheel level so the trailer lifts as it's pushed under.

quiz.explain: A tractor pulling three trailers (triples) has the greatest chance of a crack-the-whip rollover because rearward amplification, which causes the last trailer to swing wide, increases with the number of trailers.

quiz.q: In a set of triples, the rearward amplification of about 3.5 means:
options: The rearward trailer is 3.5 times more likely to roll over than the tractor
quiz.explain: Rearward amplification of 3.5 in triples means the rear trailer is about 3.5 times more likely to roll over than the tractor in the same maneuver.

quiz.q: How can you test that air flows to all trailers?
options: Open each shut-off valve and build air pressure; you should hear air flowing and the gauges should build up for each trailer. Test the brakes on each trailer
quiz.explain: To confirm air flows to all trailers in a set, open the shut-off valves, build up air pressure, and test the brakes on each trailer. All should apply and release properly.

quiz.q: What is a converter dolly?
options: A device (chassis with a fifth wheel and drawbar) with one or two axles used to couple a second or third trailer to the tractor in doubles/triples combinations
quiz.explain: A converter dolly is a chassis with one or two axles, a fifth wheel, and a drawbar used to couple a second or third trailer behind the first in doubles or triples combinations.

quiz.q: What three methods can you use to secure a second trailer before coupling?

quiz.q: What do you check when making a visual check of coupling?

quiz.q: Why should you pull a dolly out from under a trailer before you disconnect it from the trailer in front?
options: So you can reach and operate the shut-off valves and avoid damaging the dolly, trailer, or air lines during uncoupling

quiz.q: What should you check for when inspecting the converter dolly? The pintle hook?
options: Check the converter dolly for secure mounting, tires, air lines, glad hands, safety chains, and lights; check the pintle hook for wear, damage, and secure mounting
quiz.explain: Inspect the converter dolly for secure mounting, tires and wheels, air lines, glad hands, safety chains, couplers, and lights. Inspect the pintle hook for worn, damaged, or missing parts and a secure mount.

Only the middle should be closed
quiz.explain: All shut-off valves should be open except those at the back of the last trailer, which should be closed. The valves on the first trailer of doubles and the middle trailer of triples stay open.

options: Dollies built on or after March 1, 1998 are required to have an ABS indicator lamp on the left side; older units may have the ECU and wheel speed sensor wires under the unit
quiz.explain: Converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998 must have an ABS lamp on the left side. For older dollies, look under the vehicle for the ECU and wheel speed sensor wires.

quiz.q: What three methods can you use to secure a
options: second trailer before coupling: wheel chocks, parking brake, or spring brakes
cargo load: straps, chains, and ropes
tractor: air lines, brakes, and keys
quiz.explain: To secure a second trailer before coupling, use wheel chocks, the parking brake, or the trailer's spring brakes.

title: Tank Vehicles
summary: High center of gravity, liquid surge, baffles, and outage — the physics of hauling bulk liquid.

topics.heading: High center of gravity
bullets: Liquid tankers are especially easy to roll over — tests have shown they can tip even at the posted speed limit for a curve.
Take highway curves and on/off ramps well BELOW the posted speed.

topics.heading: Liquid surge
bullets: Liquid surge (the wave of liquid moving in a partially full tank) can push a stopped truck forward, even shoving it into an intersection on a slippery surface.
Baffled tanks have internal bulkheads with holes that reduce forward-and-back surge, but not side-to-side surge.
Unbaffled ('smooth bore') tanks — often used for food-grade liquids because sanitation rules forbid baffles — have the strongest surge of all. Be extra cautious starting and stopping.

topics.heading: Outage
bullets: Outage is the deliberate empty space left in a tank so the liquid has room to expand as it warms.
How much to load depends on three things: how much the liquid will expand, its weight, and legal weight limits.

topics.heading: Driving technique
bullets: Start, slow down, stop, turn, and change lanes smoothly — abrupt inputs plus surge is a bad combination.
Brake early, keep steady pressure, and increase your following distance.
Empty tank vehicles can actually take longer to stop than full ones.

quiz.q: Liquid tankers can roll over:
options: Only if going far over the speed limit
Even at the posted speed limit for a curve

quiz.q: What is 'liquid surge'?
options: The forward-and-back or side-to-side movement of liquid in a partially full tank
A type of brake fade specific to tankers

quiz.q: Baffled tanks help control:
Why do many food-grade liquid tankers use unbaffled ('smooth bore') tanks?
options: Sanitation rules make baffles too hard to clean
They're required by DOT for all tankers

quiz.q: Outage refers to:
options: Deliberately leaving room in the tank for liquid to expand
The maximum legal weight of a tanker

quiz.q: How much liquid you can load into a tank depends on:
options: Expansion amount, liquid weight, and legal weight limits
Only the color of the placard

quiz.q: Compared to full tankers, empty tank vehicles:
options: Can actually take longer to stop
Are exempt from stopping distance rules

quiz.q: The recommended way to take curves and ramps in a tank vehicle is to:
options: Go slightly above the posted speed for momentum
Go well below the posted speed
Speed depends only on tank color

quiz.q: Which driving habit is most important with a partially loaded tanker?
options: Braking and turning smoothly, and starting/stopping gradually
Accelerating hard to reduce trip time

quiz.q: How are bulkheads different than baffles?
options: Bulkheads are solid walls that separate the tank into sections but do not stop liquid movement between sections; baffles are partial walls with holes that slow liquid movement (surge)
Baffles are solid, bulkheads have holes
Bulkheads are on the outside, baffles inside
quiz.explain: Bulkheads are solid walls dividing the tank into compartments. Baffles are partial walls with openings that slow liquid surge from front to back as the vehicle moves.

quiz.q: Should a tank vehicle take curves, on ramps, or off ramps at the posted speed limits?
options: No, tank vehicles should slow down well below posted speed limits for curves, ramps, and off ramps because liquid surge and the high center of gravity increase rollover risk
Yes, always at the posted limit
quiz.explain: A safe speed on a curve for most vehicles may be too fast for a tanker. Slow down before curves, ramps, and off ramps on account of surge and the high center of gravity.

quiz.q: How are smooth bore tankers different to drive than those with baffles?
options: Smooth bore tankers have no baffles, so liquid surges more freely and they are harder to control; they need extra care to avoid surge-related control problems
quiz.explain: Smooth bore tankers have no baffles to slow liquid movement, so the liquid surges more and the tanker is harder to control. This is why some tanks are divided into compartments using bulkheads.

quiz.q: What three things determine how much liquid you can load?
options: The weight of the liquid, the amount of liquid the law allows based on vehicle weight limits, and the space needed for expansion (outage)
quiz.explain: How much liquid you can load depends on the weight of the liquid, the legal weight limit for the vehicle, and the space needed for liquid expansion (outage) as it warms.

quiz.q: What is outage?
options: The space left empty in a tank to allow the liquid to expand without overflowing as it warms
The tank being out of service
quiz.explain: Outage is the space left empty in a tank to allow the liquid room to expand as it warms, so it does not overflow or cause pressure problems.

quiz.q: How can you help control surge?
options: Keep the tank as full as possible (with proper outage) because compartment baffles and a full tank reduce the amount of free-moving liquid, and slow down and avoid sudden stops and starts
quiz.explain: Surge is the forward-and-back motion of liquid. It is hardest to control when the tank is partly full. Keep the tank reasonably full (with proper outage), slow down gradually, and avoid sudden stops and starts.

quiz.q: What two reasons make special care necessary when driving tank vehicles?
options: The high center of gravity of the liquid cargo and the surge/free surface effect that makes the vehicle harder to control
The vehicle is wider and harder to park
quiz.explain: Tank vehicles need special care because the liquid cargo has a high center of gravity (increasing rollover risk) and because surge makes the vehicle harder to control.

quiz.q: How are smooth bore tankers different to
options: drive than those with baffles? They have no baffles, so liquid surges more and they are harder to control
quiz.explain: Smooth bore tankers have no baffles to slow liquid movement, so the liquid surges more freely and the tanker is more difficult to control than one with baffles.

title: Hazardous Materials
summary: Hazard classes, shipping papers, placarding tables, and the driving/parking rules for hauling hazmat.

topics.heading: Why the rules exist
bullets: Contain the material (packaging rules for shippers, loading/unloading rules for drivers).
Communicate the risk (shipping papers, labels, placards).
Ensure safe drivers and equipment (endorsement, training, background checks).

topics.heading: The 9 hazard classes
bullets: 1 — Explosives (dynamite, fireworks)
2 — Gases (propane, oxygen, helium)
3 — Flammable liquids (gasoline)
4 — Flammable solids (matches)
5 — Oxidizers (ammonium nitrate, hydrogen peroxide)
6 — Poisons/toxic materials (pesticides, arsenic)
7 — Radioactive materials (uranium, plutonium)
8 — Corrosives (battery fluid, hydrochloric acid)
9 — Miscellaneous hazardous materials (asbestos, formaldehyde)
Plus ORM-D (other regulated material, like hairspray) and combustible liquids, which aren't numbered classes.

topics.heading: Shipping papers
bullets: Hazardous entries must be identified: entered first, highlighted, or marked with an X (or RQ for a reportable quantity) in the hazmat column.
Identification numbers are 4 digits, preceded by 'UN' or 'NA'.
Keep shipping papers within reach with your seat belt fastened, in a driver's-door pouch, or on the driver's seat when you're out of the vehicle.

topics.heading: Placarding basics
bullets: Placards must be at least 9.84 inches (250mm) square, diamond-shaped, and appear on all 4 sides: front, rear, both sides — 4 identical placards minimum.
Table 1 materials need placards for ANY amount you're carrying.
Table 2 materials only need placards once you're carrying 1,001 lbs or more total (across all shipping papers for that hazard class).

A 'DANGEROUS' placard can substitute for individual Table 2 placards when you have 1,001+ lbs total from two or more Table 2 classes, but no single class reaches 2,205 lbs (in which case you must use that class's specific placard).

topics.heading: Loading rules
bullets: Never smoke, or let anyone smoke, around Classes 1, 2.1, 3, 4, or 5 while loading or unloading.
Secure every hazardous materials package against movement.
Never transfer hazardous materials between packages while in transit (you may empty a cargo tank, but not other packages).

topics.heading: Driving & parking rules
bullets: A placarded vehicle must stop between 15 and 50 feet before a railroad crossing — same as passenger buses.
Never park a placarded vehicle within 300 feet of an open fire.
A person attending a parked placarded vehicle must be in the vehicle (awake, not in the sleeper) or within 100 feet with the vehicle in clear view.
Placarded power units must carry a fire extinguisher rated at least 10 B:C.
A 'safe haven' is an approved location where you may leave an explosives-laden vehicle unattended.
Never use burning flares or fuses near a flammable-liquid/gas tank or an explosives-laden vehicle — use reflective triangles or electric lights instead.

topics.heading: In an emergency
bullets: The Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG) is indexed by shipping name and identification number — first responders rely on it, so accurate paperwork saves lives.
At a hazmat scene: keep people away and upwind, warn others, call for help, and hand over your shipping papers to responders.

options: Reflective triangles or electric lights, never open flame

quiz.q: What is a 'safe haven' in hazmat terms?
options: A rest stop with free coffee

options: Proper shipping name and identification number

options: An approved site for parking vehicles transporting hazardous materials, authorized by FMCSA or local authorities

quiz.explain: A safe haven is an approved area (authorized by FMCSA or local authorities) for parking vehicles transporting hazardous materials.

options: You cannot park on the roadway
quiz.explain: Never park with Division 1.2 or 1.3 explosives within five feet of the traveled part of the road.

quiz.q: How close can you park to a bridge, tunnel, or building with Division 1.2 or 1.3 materials?
quiz.explain: Except for short periods needed for vehicle operation necessities, do not park within 300 feet of a bridge, tunnel, building, place where people gather, or an open fire.

quiz.q: What type of fire extinguisher must placarded vehicles carry?
quiz.explain: Placarded vehicles must carry a B:C rated fire extinguisher, sized per the regulations, for fighting electrical and flammable-liquid fires.

quiz.q: You're hauling 100 pounds of Division 4.3 (dangerous when wet) materials. Do you need to stop before a railroad-highway crossing?
options: No, Division 4.3 is not on the list of materials requiring a mandatory stop
Stop only if you smell gas

quiz.explain: Division 4.3 (dangerous when wet) is not among the hazardous materials classes that require a mandatory stop before a railroad-highway crossing.

quiz.q: At a rest area you discover your hazardous materials shipments slowly leaking from the vehicle. There is no phone around. What should you do?
options: Follow your company's emergency plan and contact the shipper or carrier immediately; if necessary, move to a safe location and call for help
Wait for a phone to become available
quiz.explain: If hazmat is leaking, follow your emergency plan and contact the shipper or carrier and emergency response as soon as possible. Never try to neutralize the leak yourself unless trained.

quiz.q: What is the Emergency Response Guide (ERG) indexed by?
options: Hazard class and ID number (and by material name)
quiz.explain: The Emergency Response Guide is indexed by the hazard class and the four-digit ID number, and also alphabetically by material name.

title: School Buses
summary: Danger zones, mirror systems, loading/unloading timing, railroad crossings, and evacuation rules.

topics.heading: The danger zone
bullets: Extends up to 30 feet from the front bumper (the first 10 feet is the most dangerous), 10 feet from each side, and 10 feet behind the rear bumper.
The left side of the bus is always considered dangerous because of passing traffic.

topics.heading: Four mirror systems
bullets: Flat mirrors (left/right front corners): should show about 200 feet (4 bus lengths) behind the bus, the sides, and the rear tires touching the ground.
Convex mirrors (below the flats): wide-angle view of the sides, but distort size and distance.
Crossover mirrors (front corners): show the danger zone directly in front of and beside the bus that you can't see directly.
Overhead inside mirror: monitors student activity inside the bus.

topics.heading: Loading timing
bullets: Activate alternating flashing amber lights about 200 feet (roughly 5-10 seconds) before the stop.
Turn on the right turn signal about 100-300 feet (roughly 3-5 seconds) before pulling over.
Stop with the front bumper at least 10 feet from the students — this forces them to walk into your view.
Put the transmission in park (or neutral) and set the parking brake at every stop.

topics.heading: Unloading & road-crossing
bullets: Have students exit and walk at least 10 feet away from the side of the bus to a point where you can plainly see them.
Students crossing in front of the bus should stop at the front-right corner, check for your signal, and cross only when you signal it's safe.
Never back a school bus with students outside of it.

topics.heading: Railroad crossings
bullets: Stop no closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet from the nearest rail.
Turn off radios and silence passengers, open the service door and driver's window, and look/listen for a train.
Cross in a low gear and never change gears while crossing.
If your bus stalls or gets trapped on the tracks, evacuate everyone immediately — move away from the tracks AND toward the direction the train would come from.

topics.heading: When you must evacuate
bullets: The bus is on fire or there's a threat of fire.
The bus is stalled on or next to a railroad crossing.
There's an imminent danger of collision, or a need to evacuate quickly because of a hazmat spill.

topics.heading: Other numbers to know
bullets: A school bus can have up to 3 feet of tail swing — check your mirrors during turns.
Backing is strongly discouraged; if unavoidable, post a lookout, signal for quiet, and back slowly.

quiz.q: How far can the danger zone extend from the front bumper of a school bus?

options: Try repeatedly to restart it before evacuating

Wait for a lookout before acting

quiz.q: Which of these requires a mandatory bus evacuation?
options: A flat tire on level ground
The bus is stalled on or adjacent to a railroad crossing

quiz.q: How much tail swing can a school bus have during a turn?
Backing a school bus with students outside of it is:
options: Fine as long as you use a lookout

quiz.q: Crossover mirrors are used to see:
options: Only the interior of the bus
The danger zone directly in front of and beside the bus, invisible to direct vision
Only the rear of the bus

quiz.q: While crossing railroad tracks in a bus, you should:
The right turn signal should be activated roughly how far before pulling over to load students?

options: The danger zone is the area around the bus where students are most at risk, extending about 10 feet from the front, sides, and rear of the bus
quiz.explain: The danger zone is the area around the bus where students are in the most danger, extending about 10 feet from the front, sides, and rear. Keep students out of this area.

quiz.q: What should you be able to see if the outside flat mirrors are adjusted properly? The outside convex mirrors? The crossover mirrors?
options: Flat mirrors: the side of the bus and rear tires; convex mirrors: a wider area including the danger zone; crossover mirrors: the front bumper area and ground directly in front of the bus
All mirrors show the same view
quiz.explain: Proper flat mirrors show the side of the bus and the rear tires. Convex mirrors show a wider area including the danger zone. Crossover mirrors show the front bumper and the ground directly in front of the bus.

quiz.q: You are loading students along the route. When should you activate your alternating flashing amber warning lights?
options: You should activate them at least 200 feet before the stop so approaching drivers are warned
quiz.explain: Activate the alternating flashing amber warning lights at least 200 feet before the bus stop so other drivers know to slow down and prepare to stop.

quiz.q: You are unloading students along your route. Where should students walk to after exiting the bus?
options: Students should go to a point at least 10 feet in front of the bus, walk to the left of the bus, and wait for the driver's signal before crossing
Students should cross directly behind the bus
Students should stay on the bus
quiz.explain: After exiting, students should move at least 10 feet in front of the bus, out of the danger zone and into the driver's view, and wait for the driver's signal before crossing.

quiz.q: After unloading at school, why should you walk through the bus?
options: To be sure no students are left on the bus or sleeping, and to check for items and hazards before driving away
quiz.explain: After unloading, walk through the bus to make sure no students are left behind (some may be sleeping or hidden) and to check for hazards before driving away.

quiz.q: What position should students be in front of the bus before they cross the roadway?
options: At least 10 feet directly in front of the bus, out of the danger zone and in plain view of the driver
Right in front of the bumper
quiz.explain: Students should be at least 10 feet directly in front of the bus, in the driver's full view and out of the danger zone, before being signaled to cross.

quiz.q: Under what conditions must you evacuate the bus?
options: When there is danger of fire, the bus is in the path of a train or other danger, or when it is unsafe to remain in the bus (e.g., fire, collision, or hazardous spill)
Only when the driver says so regardless of danger
quiz.explain: Evacuate the bus when there is danger of fire, when the bus is in danger from a train or other traffic, or when it is otherwise unsafe to remain in the bus.

quiz.q: How far from the nearest rail should you stop at a highway-rail crossing?
options: Between 15 and 50 feet from the nearest rail, with the bus in a position to see the tracks clearly
At the edge of the rail
quiz.explain: Stop between 15 and 50 feet from the nearest rail so you can see both directions along the tracks before proceeding.

quiz.q: What is a passive highway-rail crossing? Why should you be extra cautious at this type of crossing?
options: A crossing with no gates, flashing lights, or bells - only passive warning signs. You must be extra cautious because there is no active signal to warn you of a train, so you must look and listen yourself
quiz.explain: A passive crossing has no active warning devices, only signs. Because there is no signal to warn you, you must slow down, look, and listen for approaching trains before crossing.

quiz.q: How should you use your brakes if your vehicle is equipped with antilock brakes (ABS)?
options: Brake the same way you always have; in an emergency with working ABS on all axles you can fully apply the brakes
quiz.explain: With ABS, brake normally. Pumping the brakes defeats ABS - apply steady, firm pressure. In an emergency with ABS on all axles you can fully apply the brakes.

quiz.q: You are loading students along the route.
options: Activate the alternating flashing amber warning lights at least 200 feet before the stop
Turn the emergency flashers on after loading
Blow the horn at the stop
quiz.explain: Activate the amber warning lights at least 200 feet before the stop so approaching traffic is warned.

quiz.q: After unloading at school, why should you
options: walk through the bus? To make sure no students are left behind and to check for hazards
start the engine? To warm the bus
close the windows? To secure the bus
quiz.explain: Walk through the bus after unloading to be sure no students are left on board and to check for hazards before moving.

quiz.q: How far from the nearest rail should you
options: stop at a highway-rail crossing? Between 15 and 50 feet from the nearest rail
quiz.explain: Stop between 15 and 50 feet from the nearest rail at a highway-rail crossing so you can see the tracks clearly.

quiz.q: How should you use your brakes if your
options: vehicle is equipped with antilock brakes (ABS)? Brake the same way you always have, using firm steady pressure
road is wet? Pump the brakes
quiz.explain: With ABS, brake normally with firm steady pressure. Don't pump the brakes, as this defeats ABS. You can fully apply the brakes in an emergency.

title: Vehicle Inspection Test
examFocus: Pre-trip inspection — practice after you get your permit and start trucking school
summary: What the examiner watches for during the hands-on pre-trip inspection, including the exact numbers for the brake checks.

topics.heading: How the test works
bullets: You must point to or touch each item, name it, and explain to the examiner what you're checking and why.
A vehicle with components that are labeled or marked cannot be used for this test.
This test must be passed before you can move on to the basic control skills test.

topics.heading: Engine compartment & cab checks
bullets: Check for leaks, belt condition (1/2 to 3/4 inch play), oil level, coolant level, and power steering fluid — all with the engine off.
After starting: oil pressure should rise to normal quickly, air pressure should build toward governor cut-out (about 120-140 psi), and warning lights/buzzers should go out.

topics.heading: The hydraulic brake check (if applicable)
bullets: Pump the brake pedal 3 times, then hold it down for 5 seconds — the pedal must not move. Skipping either step is an automatic failure of this part of the test.

topics.heading: The air brake check (3 parts, if applicable)
bullets: 1) With air built to governor cutoff, release parking brake and hold the foot brake for 1 minute — leak must be under 3 psi/minute (single vehicle) or 4 psi/minute (combination).
2) Fan the brakes on and off — the low air warning must activate before pressure drops below 55 psi.
3) Keep fanning — the tractor protection valve/parking brake valve must pop out (close) somewhere in the 20-45 psi range.
Skipping any of these three steps is an automatic failure of this part of the test.

topics.heading: External walk-around highlights
bullets: Tread depth: 4/32 inch minimum on steering tires, 2/32 inch on all others.
Check every axle's suspension, brakes, and wheels the same way — springs, mounts, shock absorbers, slack adjusters, and brake drums/linings.
On combination vehicles: inspect the fifth wheel for grease, a closed gap, properly seated locking jaws, and secure air/electric lines.

title: Basic Vehicle Control Skills Test
examFocus: Backing exercises — practice after you get your permit and start trucking school
summary: The maneuvering exercises and how they're scored — encroachments, pull-ups, and 'looks.'

topics.heading: Possible exercises
bullets: Straight line backing.
Offset back to the right, and offset back to the left.
Parallel park (driver's side, and conventional).
Alley dock.

topics.heading: How scoring works
bullets: Encroachments: touching or crossing a boundary line or cone — each one counts as an error.
Pull-ups: stopping and pulling forward to reposition. Initial pull-ups aren't penalized, but too many count against you.

Outside vehicle observations ('looks'): you may exit to check your position, but must place the vehicle in neutral, set the parking brake, and exit safely (three points of contact). You get a maximum of 2 looks — except straight line backing, which allows only 1.
Final position: you must end each exercise exactly as instructed, or you'll be penalized and could fail.
